explanation: First four arguments of the system call, stored in hexadecimal. Useful for reconstructing what a process was trying to do.
Arguments to an execve syscall (can be more than four).
User’s account name under which the process ran.
Access mode of a resource assigned to a VM.
Netfilter packet disposition (or integrity policy action).
IPv4 or IPv6 address (often follows a hostname field).
CPU architecture of the system (e.g. c000003e = x86_64).
Number of arguments to an execve syscall.
Audit User ID (loginuid). Assigned at login and never changes, even after su/sudo. Most reliable identity field.
Banners used on a printed page.
Name of the subsystem bus a VM resource belongs to.
Number of bits used when setting a Linux capability.
Resource category assigned to a VM.
Path to the cgroup that contained the process when the event was generated.
Name of the crypto cipher selected.
Resource class assigned to a VM.
Full command line executed. Especially useful with interpreters (exe may show /bin/bash while cmd shows the real script + args).
Short command name (basename of the executable or script).
Current working directory of the process when the system call was invoked.
Data associated with TTY records (often hex-encoded keystrokes).
Major:minor device numbers (path records) or device name as found in /dev (AVC).
Effective Group ID of the process.
Number of entries in a netfilter table.
Error code of the audited operation.
Effective User ID of the process.
Full path to the executable that was invoked.
Exit / return code of the system call. Use ausearch -i --exit to decode.
Netfilter protocol / address family (IPv4 or IPv6).
File-system name flags or mmap flags.
File assigned effective capability map (short form).
File assigned inherited capability map (short form).
File permitted capability map or crypto key fingerprint.
File-system Group ID of the process.
File-system User ID of the process.
Real Group ID of the process.
PAM modules that approved the action.
Netfilter hook the packet came from.
Hostname associated with the event (often the remote host).
User ID of an account that was changed.
Network address of a printer (or instruction pointer in seccomp).
Inode number of the referenced file/directory.
Group ID of the inode’s owner.
User ID of the inode’s owner.
Request argument to the ioctl syscall.
Which item (path record) is being recorded.
Number of PATH records attached to this event.
Arbitrary string attached to the audit rule that generated the event. Extremely useful for filtering.
Server or client in a crypto operation.
Key size used in a crypto operation.
Timestamp + unique event ID, or additional name=value pairs.
Message type for user-space AVC denials (usually from D-Bus).
Number of arguments to a socket call.
Full path of the file/directory passed as an argument.
Kind of file operation being referenced.
New value being set for a feature.
New character device assigned to a VM.
Name of a new disk resource assigned to a VM.
File system being added to a VM.
New group ID assigned to a user.
New value of a feature lock.
New value for TTY password logging.
New amount of memory (KB) assigned to a VM.
MAC address of a new network interface assigned to a VM.
Device name of an RNG being added to a VM.
New number of virtual CPUs assigned to a VM.
PID of the netlink packet sender.
Audit UID of the user who originally logged in and started the target process (OBJ_PID records only).
SELinux context of the object (the thing being acted upon).
High SELinux sensitivity level of the object.
Low SELinux sensitivity level of the object.
SELinux user associated with the object.
Flags passed to the open syscall.
Group ID of the object’s owner.
Command name of the target process (OBJ_PID records only).
Previous / present value of a kernel feature or audit setting.
Previous character device assigned to a VM.
Previous disk resource of a VM.
Previous file system of a VM.
Previous value of a feature lock.
Previous memory allocation of a VM.
Previous MAC address of a VM network interface.
Previous RNG device of a VM.
Previous value of an SELinux boolean.
Previous number of virtual CPUs of a VM.
Operation being performed that is audited.
Process ID of the target process (OBJ_PID records only).
Session ID of the target process (OBJ_PID records only).
Real user ID of the target process / object owner.
Process ambient / effective / inherited / permitted capability maps.
Inode number of the parent file.
Full path of the file/directory (especially in AVC events).
File permission that triggered the event (read/write/execute/attribute).
File permission mask that triggered a watch event.
Whether SELinux is in permissive mode.
Process ID (userspace) or Thread ID (kernel). For single-threaded processes they are equal. This is the kernel TID (gettid), not a pthread_t.
Quantity of bytes of an IPC object.
Text string explaining the reason for the action.
New MAC context assigned to a session.
Session ID from which the process was started.
Signal number that caused abnormal termination.
Resulting state of the audit daemon configuration.
SELinux context of the subject (the actor).
SELinux user associated with the subject.
Whether the system call succeeded (yes) or failed (no).
Numeric system-call number that was executed.
Controlling terminal device. Value (none) means no controlling terminal.
The audit record’s type (SYSCALL, PATH, EXECVE, AVC, etc.).
Real User ID of the process.
Generic value associated with the operation (or new SELinux boolean value).
Name of the virtual machine from which the event originated.
File name in a watch record.
